misconceptions.description: Naming a theory next to a design decision and treating the citation itself as the justification, with no link between the principle and the choice
misconceptions.trigger: defense says 'this aligns with cognitive load theory' but does not say which design element the principle changed
misconceptions.feedback: A theoretical defense connects a specific principle to a specific design element and explains the mechanism. A citation alone is decoration.

misconceptions.description: Choosing the design first on intuition, then bolting on a theory at defense time to rationalize a decision the theory never informed
misconceptions.trigger: the design would be identical if the cited theory were removed
misconceptions.feedback: Test whether the theory did work: if removing it would not change the design, it was rationalization, not a defense.

misconceptions.description: Invoking a theory principle that does not actually apply to the design move, such as citing the redundancy principle to justify adding more on-screen text
misconceptions.trigger: the cited principle predicts the opposite of the choice made
misconceptions.feedback: Check the direction of the principle. If the principle would predict the opposite choice, you have cited it against yourself.

misconceptions.description: Presenting one supporting theory while ignoring a well-known tension or competing principle a committee will raise
misconceptions.trigger: defense cites only confirming theory and never addresses a known trade-off
misconceptions.feedback: Name the competing principle and explain why your context favors one over the other; a one-sided defense invites the obvious counter-question.
